rzzzt · Oct 17, 2026

The README mentions floooh's implementation which is a bit more simplified, there is no complete netlist so the smaller TTL glue chips will not be considered. It does work in real time though. The common interface between emulated ICs is a 64-bit integer that maps logic levels of interest at a given simulation step to its individual bits:

- https://github.com/floooh/chips/blob/master/README.md

- https://github.com/floooh/chips/blob/9e88298ce56319953ac7a43...

- https://floooh.github.io/tiny8bit/player.html?id=c64&dbg=1 (use the "Hardware" menu to get activity views similar to Salvatore's emulator)

varispeed · Oct 17, 2026

> Please note that even on fast computers this program struggles to simulate the C64 hardware at real speed. A real C64 is simulated at 31% of its speed on an Apple M3 Max, 39% on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495 (Gorgon Halo), and 48% on an Apple M5 Max

Key takeaway is why FPGA is still useful. Even modern CPUs can't handle certain seemingly simple data processing tasks in realtime.

linker3000 · Oct 17, 2026

This is really cool, and a fantastic piece of work. It may come in handy when diagnosing / fixing C64 boards.

Stretch goals:

* Allow the simulation to run diagnostics carts.

* On the 250407 board I have had timing edge cases with PLA replacements - the fix is often to fit a small (100pF) capacitor on the /CASRAM line to slow it down a bit. The cap is fitted from the left leg of an existing 82 Ohm resistor and a nearby ground point close to 'RAM6'. Some boards actually have official space for the capacitor - designated C204. With some original PLA variants on real boards the capacitor may already be fitted. It would be good to be able to enable and disable this capacitor and set its value to see the effects.

Write-up: https://linker3000.com/index.php/blog/poor64

tombert · Oct 17, 2026

I remember Byuu (RIP) wrote an article around ~10 years ago talking about why BSNES/Higan was "slow", explaining that it's really not slow given what it's trying to do. The more accurately you simulate the chips, there is simply more over overhead involved with synchronization and whatnot.

I remember in that article they mentioned a Pong circuit simulation like this that was getting something along the lines of 10FPS of gameplay, which astonished me. You don't get a lot simpler of a game than Pong and even on amazing hardware it was still unplayable if you want the truest form of emulation.
